subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 11 periods = 440 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

periods.activity_title: Meeting Officer Bharat's Road Safety Letter

time_bands.activity: Open textbook to pages 25–27. Ask children what they notice about the page layout — does it look like a story, a poem, or a letter? Take two or three responses to activate curiosity about the genre.
Read the full letter aloud expressively, pausing briefly after each numbered rule. Point to the accompanying illustration for each rule so children connect text to image.

Invite students to read the letter again quietly and underline any word they find unfamiliar. Briefly explain the four 'New Words' — pedestrian, footpath, reflective, distract — using examples from the letter itself.
Ask the class to count the six rules on their fingers as you name them together. Pair-share: each child tells their partner which rule they think is most important and why, in one sentence.

periods.teacher_notes: The letter is addressed directly to children, so reading it in Officer Bharat's warm, caring voice helps students feel its personal tone. Watch for confusion between 'reflective' (bouncing light back) and 'reflect' (to think) — the road-safety context anchors the correct sense. The New Words box on the text pages is a useful anchor; tap it often during the read-aloud.

periods.activity_title: Comprehension Discussion — Safety Rules in Detail

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — A. (p.28): answer three short-answer questions on road-safety rules.

time_bands.activity: Invite three volunteers to name any one road-safety rule from Officer Bharat's letter from memory. Affirm correct recalls and gently correct any misremembering by pointing back to the text.

Work through Let us Think — A. (p.28) as a whole-class discussion. Pose each question orally, give thinking time, then invite responses. Guide students to frame answers in complete sentences grounded in the text.
Students write their answers to all three questions in their notebooks. Circulate and support phrasing, particularly for question 3 which asks for a reason.
Select two or three notebooks and read aloud exemplary answers. Discuss what makes a good short answer — a clear reason tied to the letter's words.

periods.teacher_notes: Question 3 (holding an adult's hand) requires students to give a reason rather than recall a fact, so model a sentence starter such as 'We should hold an adult's hand because…' if children struggle to move beyond single-word answers. Having read Officer Bharat's letter together earlier, students can return to the text for evidence — encourage this habit from the start.

periods.activity_title: True or False — Judging Road Safety Statements

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — B. (p.28): judge six true-or-false statements about road safety rules.

time_bands.activity: Write one sample statement on the board: 'It is safe to cross the road anywhere you like.' Ask students to give a thumbs-up for true or thumbs-down for false, then call on one student to correct the false statement using Officer Bharat's letter.

Work through Let us Think — B. (p.28) statement by statement. Read each one aloud; students write T or F in their notebooks, then the class discusses the answer together, locating the supporting evidence in the letter.
For each false statement, students rewrite it as a correct, true sentence. Encourage them to borrow exact phrases from the letter to make their corrections precise.

Quick whole-class share-out: one student reads their corrected version of statement 4 (dark clothes) and one reads their corrected version of statement 5 (playing near road). Class evaluates whether the correction is accurate.

periods.teacher_notes: Statement 4 — 'Wearing dark clothes in the evening makes you more visible' — is a common confusion; the letter's Rule 5 specifies reflective stickers precisely because dark clothes do the opposite. Use this as the anchor for a brief discussion on why reflective material works. Encourage students to cite the rule number when they justify their answers.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — C. (pp.28–29): choose the correct option for three road-safety questions.
Let us Think — D. (pp.29–30): identify eleven road/safety signs and write their meanings.

time_bands.activity: Ask students whether they have seen any road signs on their way to school. Accept two or three examples and briefly explain that signs help everyone on the road communicate without words.

Read each multiple-choice question from Let us Think — C. (pp.28–29) aloud. Students discuss their choice with a neighbour, then write the answer in their notebooks. Review each answer with the class, linking it back to Officer Bharat's rules.

Open to Let us Think — D. (pp.29–30). Teacher walks through each of the eleven signs using the help box, naming the sign and miming or describing its meaning. Students then write the meaning beside each symbol in their textbooks.

Quick quiz: teacher points to any three of the eleven signs on the page and cold-calls students to say the meaning from memory. Celebrate correct answers and note any signs the class found tricky for a brief revision.

periods.teacher_notes: Many students will recognise the 'School Ahead' and 'No Honking' signs from daily experience; use those familiar ones as entry points before moving to less common signs like 'U-turn' or 'Drive Slow'. The help box on the textbook page is a scaffold — encourage students to try from memory first before consulting it.

periods.activity_title: Talking Road Safety — Guided Conversation on Rules

time_bands.activity: Set the scenario: 'Imagine a younger child from Class I asks you — How do I cross the road safely? What would you say?' Give students a moment to think, then take two or three opening responses to warm up the conversation.

Organise students into pairs. One partner plays the younger child who asks questions about crossing the road; the other plays the older guide who explains Officer Bharat's rules. Circulate, prompt with cue cards naming each of the six rules, and encourage full sentences.
Switch roles within pairs. The guide now asks: 'What should I do if it is dark outside?' — requiring the partner to explain Rule 5 (reflective stickers) in their own words.
Two or three pairs perform their exchange for the class. After each performance, the class gives one positive comment and suggests one improvement in clarity or completeness.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read and discussed Officer Bharat's letter in detail, students have the language they need — the challenge here is rephrasing rules in their own words for a younger audience. Watch for students who only recite rules verbatim; prompt them gently with 'Can you say it in a different way?' to build genuine oral fluency.
materials: Cue cards listing the six rules (teacher-prepared on the board or card strips)

periods.activity_title: Safe or Unsafe — Classify and Spot Errors

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — A. (p.30): classify five activities as safe or unsafe.
Let us Write — B. (p.31): spot six road-safety errors in the picture.

time_bands.activity: Ask the class: 'Name one thing you do every day near a road that is safe, and one that might be unsafe.' Accept a few responses to activate thinking before the written task.

Guide students through Let us Write — A. (p.30). Read each of the five activities aloud together. Students discuss with a partner whether each is safe or unsafe, then write their classification with a brief reason (one phrase is enough) in their notebooks.

Turn to the picture in Let us Write — B. (p.31). Teacher leads a picture walk — describe what you see together. Students work individually to list the six errors they spot, writing each as a short statement (e.g. 'The person is using headphones near traffic').
Whole-class share: one student reads one error they found. Other students raise their hand if they found the same error. Work through all six errors together to confirm the complete list.

periods.teacher_notes: Task B (spotting errors) is rich in inferential demand — students must apply Officer Bharat's six rules as criteria for judging what is wrong in the scene. Prompt any student who is stuck by asking: 'Check Rule 1 — does this picture follow it?' The error about the traffic light state (green for pedestrians versus green for vehicles) is the trickiest; spend a moment there.

periods.activity_title: Modelled Writing — A Thank-You Letter to Officer Bharat

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — D. (unspecified page): write a thank-you letter to the traffic police using the given starter.

time_bands.activity: Revisit the format of Officer Bharat's letter on textbook pages 25–27 — point out the greeting, the body paragraphs, and the closing. Explain that today the class will write back to Officer Bharat, using the same letter format.

Model the letter aloud on the board, writing the provided starter and thinking aloud: 'What rules have I understood? I want to promise I will follow them — which ones mean most to me?' Write two model sentences that name specific rules from the chapter.

Students write their own letter in notebooks, using the starter provided in the textbook. They must name at least two specific rules from Officer Bharat's letter and write a personal promise. Circulate and give brief oral feedback on clarity and completeness.
Two volunteers read their letters aloud. The class listens and gives a one-word reaction (e.g. 'clear', 'warm', 'detailed'). Remind students to sign their name and grade as the letter instructs.

periods.teacher_notes: The starter sentence in the textbook ends with 'I have read your letter carefully and understood that…' — students must complete this with specific content from Officer Bharat's rules, not vague phrases. Praise letters that name concrete rules (e.g. 'I understood that reflective stickers help drivers see me in the dark') over generic ones. Keep letters short — two or three body sentences is appropriate for Grade IV.

periods.activity_title: Countable and Uncountable Nouns — Food Words First

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — A. (p.32): classify fourteen food-related words as countable or uncountable.

time_bands.activity: Write 'apple' and 'water' on the board. Ask: 'Can you count apples? Can you count water?' Draw out the idea that some things we count and some we measure or name in bulk. Introduce the grammar terms 'countable' and 'uncountable' using the box on page 32.

Work through Let us Learn — A. (p.32) together. Read each word aloud and ask students to say 'C' or 'U' chorally, then write it in their notebooks. Pause on tricky pairs — 'coffee' (U) versus 'coffee jars' (C) and 'potatoes' (C) versus 'mashed potatoes' (U) — and discuss why the form changes the category.

Students revisit the completed list and write one original sentence using any three of the words — one countable, one uncountable, and one of their choice — to show they understand the distinction in use.

Quick check: teacher calls out any three words from the list at random and students hold up a 'C' or 'U' card (or write on a slate/scrap paper). Celebrate correct responses and note persistent errors for brief clarification.

periods.teacher_notes: The most productive teaching moment in this task is the 'coffee / coffee jars' contrast — the same substance becomes countable when placed in a container. Link this to everyday experience ('I can count three jars, but I cannot count coffee itself') to make the concept concrete. Avoid treating the C/U distinction as a list to memorise; ground every decision in the question 'Can I put a number directly before this word?'
materials: Scrap paper or slates for the quick check

periods.activity_title: Road-Safety Words — Countable and Uncountable Classification

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — B. (p.33): classify eleven road-safety vocabulary words as countable or uncountable.
Let us Learn — C. (p.33): underline countable and circle uncountable nouns in the banana milkshake recipe.

time_bands.activity: Recall the countable/uncountable distinction explored with food words. Write 'helmet' and 'traffic' on the board and ask students to decide which is which and explain their reasoning. Use this to bridge into road-safety vocabulary.

Students complete Let us Learn — B. (p.33) individually, sorting the eleven road-safety words into two columns in their notebooks. Review answers as a class, paying extra attention to 'speed', 'safety', and 'fuel' which students may find counter-intuitive.

Read the banana milkshake recipe for Let us Learn — C. (p.33) together as a class. Students then work individually — underlining countable nouns and circling uncountable nouns directly in the text. Pairs compare and reconcile any differences.

Quick share: ask students to name all the uncountable nouns they found in the recipe. List them on the board and confirm. Ask: 'What would happen if you tried to count milk or honey individually?' to reinforce understanding through humour.

periods.teacher_notes: Having applied the countable/uncountable distinction to food words, students are now applying the same skill to road-safety vocabulary — the same grammatical concept in a new domain reinforces transfer. 'Speed', 'safety', and 'transportation' are abstract uncountable nouns; if students are puzzled, ask 'Can I have three speeds or three safeties?' to make the test concrete and a little playful.

periods.activity_title: Safe and Unsafe Choices — Picture Error Hunt

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do — A. (p.30): classify five road-side activities as safe or unsafe.
Let us Do — B. (p.31): identify and list six road-safety errors in the busy road picture.

time_bands.activity: Ask students to close their eyes and imagine walking to school. What road-related things do they see or do? Take a few responses. Explain that the tasks ahead ask them to judge which everyday actions are safe and which are dangerous, using Officer Bharat's six rules as a checklist.

Students complete Let us Do — A. (p.30) by classifying the five activities into two columns — 'Safe' and 'Unsafe' — in their notebooks. Partners compare their columns and discuss any disagreement. Whole-class review to confirm answers.

Open to the busy road picture on page 31 (Let us Do — B.). Pairs examine the picture carefully and write down every error they spot, naming the unsafe behaviour and the rule it breaks. Encourage full sentences: 'The child is walking on the road — this breaks Rule 3.'
Groups share one error each in turn until all six are on the board. Discuss: 'Which error do you think is the most dangerous and why?' — one or two students share a brief opinion.

periods.teacher_notes: Having written about safe and unsafe behaviours in the writing unit, students now approach the same content through observation and critical analysis of a visual. This shift from producing text to reading a complex image stretches thinking — encourage students to look systematically (top-to-bottom, left-to-right) rather than randomly to ensure they find all six errors. If pairs find only four or five, prompt them to check the sky (traffic light state) and the road markings.

periods.activity_title: Be Smart, Be Safe — Whole-Chapter Synthesis and Celebration

time_bands.activity: Open by asking: 'What are the six road-safety rules Officer Bharat shared with us?' Take contributions from around the room until all six are named — zebra crossing, traffic lights, footpaths, holding an adult's hand, reflective stickers, and staying alert. Write each rule as a single key word on the board.

Word-work revisit: teacher calls out a mix of nouns from the chapter — pedestrian, traffic, helmet, safety, bicycle, fuel. Students write each as C or U on a slip of paper. Pairs compare, then the class confirms together. Ask one student to make a sentence using a countable noun and one using an uncountable noun from the list.

Quick-write: each student writes three sentences — one summarising what the chapter taught them, one naming the rule they will personally commit to, and one using any new vocabulary word (pedestrian, footpath, reflective, or distract) in a meaningful sentence. This is an independent short piece; no starter is provided.

Oral-presentation round: four or five students share their three sentences with the class. The class listens and gives a silent thumbs-up if the vocabulary word was used correctly. After all share, the class identifies one road-safety idea that appeared in every student's writing.

Closing reflection: the teacher asks the class to look at the road scene on page 31 one last time (without writing) and count how many errors they can spot silently in their heads. Then: 'If you were standing beside Officer Bharat today, what one piece of advice would you give a child who had never read this chapter?' — one final voice from the room.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together the grammar, vocabulary, reading comprehension, oral language, and road-safety awareness built across the chapter. The quick-write is deliberately open — it asks students to synthesise in their own words without a model or starter, which is the true test of whether understanding has been internalised. Celebrate responses that connect multiple rules or that use the new vocabulary naturally in context.

items.item_stem: Officer Bharat's letter lists six rules for staying safe on the road. Which of the following correctly describes what you should do BEFORE stepping onto a zebra crossing?

options.label: A
options.text: Look right, then left, then right again, and cross only when it is safe.

options.label: B
options.text: Run across as fast as you can.

options.label: C
options.text: Wait for a friend to cross with you first.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Suggests the student believes speed is the priority at a crossing, missing the 'look' step entirely.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reveals a social misunderstanding — the rule focuses on looking at traffic, not waiting for companions.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Indicates the student has confused urgency with safety; Officer Bharat's letter explicitly says walk calmly, never run.

items.item_stem: Officer Bharat explains in his letter why children should avoid using headphones or mobile phones near traffic. In your own words, explain what could go wrong if you use headphones while walking on the road, and name one other distraction the letter warns against.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: If you use headphones near traffic, you cannot hear the sounds of approaching vehicles, which means you may not realise a vehicle is coming and could get hurt. The letter also warns against playing near traffic as another distraction.

items.item_stem: Listen carefully. Your teacher will read a short description of a child walking home from school. Decide: is the child following Officer Bharat's road-safety rules or breaking them? Choose the correct answer.

options.text: Arjun runs across the road to reach the other side quickly.
Arjun uses his mobile phone while waiting at the traffic light.
Arjun waits for the pedestrian green signal before crossing.
Arjun walks on the footpath all the way to the zebra crossing.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statement 1 — True (footpaths are for pedestrians, Rule 3). Statement 2 — False (using a mobile phone near traffic is a distraction, Rule 6). Statement 3 — True (wait for the pedestrian green signal, Rule 2). Statement 4 — False (walk calmly, never run, Rule 2).

2. Wearing dark clothes while walking home at night.
3. Holding an adult's hand while crossing a busy road.
4. Listening to music on headphones while walking near traffic.

Error in the picture | Rule it breaks
Person using headphones near moving vehicles | ?
